narrativeProgression.description: Introduction to the concept of valence electrons and how to determine them using electron configuration.
Carbon is chosen as an example element.
The narrator provides the electron configuration of Carbon (1s2 2s2 2p2).
The narrator concludes that Carbon has four valence electrons based on its electron configuration.
The narrator explains how the highest principal quantum number determines the outer subshells and consequently the number of valence electrons.

narrativeProgression.description: Arsenic is introduced as a new example.
Narrator acknowledges the complexity of Arsenic's electron configuration while emphasizing the consistent approach.
Narrator emphasizes paying attention to the highest principal quantum number (4) in Arsenic's electron configuration.
Narrator identifies the 4s and 4p subshells as relevant for counting valence electrons.
The 3d subshell is ignored, as it is not the highest principal quantum number.
Narrator counts the electrons in the 4s and 4p subshells, concluding that Arsenic has five valence electrons.
Narrator confirms the five valence electrons by referring to Arsenic's position in the fourth period and counting the electrons in the P block.
